title: Oklahoma's Buried Meteor Crater Is 100 Million Years Younger Than Thought
summary:
Deep beneath the small town of Ames, Oklahoma, lies a giant meteor crater that stretches for miles underground. Layers of sediment now cover it, but scientists have just learned something surprising about it. The crater is nearly 100 million years younger than they believed.

For years, researchers thought the Ames crater formed about 467.5 million years ago. That would have made it part of a group of big meteor impacts across North America known as the Ordovician Meteor Event. Because so many craters seemed to date from the same time, some scientists have suggested Earth may once have had a ring of space rocks around it, a bit like Saturn's rings.

Now a team from The University of Texas at Austin has a new answer. They studied tiny crystals called zircons, found in granite rock that was changed by the impact. By dating those crystals, they found the meteor struck about 370 million years ago instead. "No matter what technique we used, it was coming back to this younger signal," said lead author Elizabeth Catlos.

So why was the old date wrong? Earlier, scientists had dated the crater using fossil teeth from an ancient eel-like animal called a conodont. Catlos said those teeth were probably already millions of years old when the meteor hit. The impact likely churned up older material and mixed the fossils into the rocks.

The team worked with NASA to image the zircons and confirm they were changed by the crash. The new date places the impact close to a mass extinction about 372 million years ago that wiped out much of the ocean's life. The study was published in July in the journal Meteoritics & Planetary Science.
why_it_matters: Correct dates for ancient impacts help scientists test ideas about Earth's history, including whether impacts are linked to mass extinctions.
